paragraphs.source_en: One of the articles closed with a quote from a professor at Washington University in St. Louis, a Pathfinder scientist working on the very same campus where I would soon be studying. I underlined his name—Ray Arvidson—and carefully tore the article from the page to send to my father, who was certainly following these distant goings-on. I hoped the fact that I would be at a university with a famous planetary scientist would make my parents feel better about the debt they were about to incur to cover the daunting gap between my scholarship and the full cost of attending.

paragraphs.source_en: Once on campus, I made a beeline for Ray’s classroom—that fall, he was teaching a course called Land Dynamics and the Environment. From there it was a short hop to his lab, where he did his pioneering Mars work. Ray was nearly fifty, a Swede who’d grown up in New Jersey. He was humble, soft-spoken, and tremendously respected, having just taken over as the department head of Earth and planetary sciences. He had a short beard that was starting to turn gray, and his eyes crinkled whenever he smiled. He specialized in remote sensing: how to get beyond your immediate environment, how to discern the nature of a place from a distance.

paragraphs.source_en: On his flickering desktop, he showed a group of us how to “see” beyond the visual wavelengths, into the ultraviolet and infrared. Computer techniques stretched and transformed orbital views into a psychedelic swath of colors. He would toggle a few settings on his display, and types of land cover that initially all looked the same would filter in and out, revealing their underlying complexity. We were astounded that by simply adjusting the wavelengths of the light he looked for, he could pinpoint dozens of rocks and minerals that had previously been hidden.

paragraphs.source_en: Ray had grown up shooting off balloon rockets in his backyard. As a graduate student at Brown University, he’d analyzed the Mariner 9 data, then worked on the Viking landers, taking over as the head of the imaging team after the first year of operations. I particularly loved listening to his stories about the Pathfinder mission.
